newsitem.title: USA: Rev. Jackson presses Donnelley with Jan. 15 deadline.
newsitem.headline: Rev. Jackson presses Donnelley with Jan. 15 deadline.

text.p: The Rev. Jesse Jackson said Monday he would press the country's most popular magazines to change printers if R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. failed to resolve discrimination lawsuits by Jan. 15, birthday of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr.

Jackson, who met with Donnelley executives for two hours seeking information on the company's work force of 39,000, also demanded changes in the company's all-white board of directors and pension fund managers.

"If by Jan. 15 there is no plan ... then we will challenge those companies (doing business with Donnelley) to choose another company," Jackson told reporters outside the downtown headquarters of the nation's largest commercial printer.

Scores of popular magazines including Time, Sports Illustrated, The New Yorker and Cosmopolitan as well as federal tax forms, telephone books and other materials are printed by Donnelley, which was hit with a $500 million class-action lawsuit last month charging the company with racial discrimination.

"These customers share some responsibility," Jackson said, without giving specifics about how he would pursue a boycott. He said affected workers deserved monetary settlements, citing recent awards won by plaintiffs who sued Texaco Inc. and Circuit City Stores for racial discrimination.
Donnelley, which has maintained it does not tolerate discrimination, issued a statement from acting Chairman and Chief Executive Officer John Richman denying the lawsuit's allegations.

"I have spent a great deal of time reviewing these allegations, as well as our employment policies and practices. We have a solid record, and we want to get to court on this matter as quickly as possible," Richman said.

Jackson, head of the Rainbow PUSH Action Network, was accompanied by several former Donnelley workers who lost their jobs in a 1994 plant closing and filed the lawsuit charging race and age discrimination against the company.
The suit claims black and older workers affected by the closing, announced in 1993, fared worse than younger white employees in getting reassinged with the company.

"I felt I as well as others were mistreated. There were jobs that I was qualified for that I didn't get," said James Adams, a 36-year black employee at Donnelley whose son was also part of the lawsuit.

Jackson, who described the tone of the meeting as "amiable," compared the workers' plight to seasonal fruit pickers and rural sharecroppers from a previous era who were never quite granted full-time jobs by their employers.

He said Donnelley was "resisting" the lawsuits, but had pledged to "speed up their search" for minority directors and pension fund managers. He said he would push for more information about the company's work force, adding that his group bought 1,000 shares of Donnelley stock to press its case at shareholder meetings.
